summary: A feature story on the Tanaka family of Tokyo's historic Asakusa District, who keep alive the Japanese New Year (Oshogatsu) traditions across generations. It walks through their rituals: Osoji cleaning, kadomatsu and shimenawa decorations, osechi ryori and toso, the Joya no Kane bell ringing at Senso-ji, karuta, and a family gathering at the kotatsu. The piece stresses that these customs are a living heritage passed on to younger generations amid globalization.
one_line: The Tanaka family of Tokyo's Asakusa District preserves Oshogatsu New Year traditions, from Osoji cleaning to Senso-ji's bell ringing, as living cultural heritage.
key_facts: The Tanaka Family lives in the historic Asakusa District of Tokyo and opened their doors to tell the story of their 'Oshogatsu' (New Year) celebrations; the story is dated 10 September 2023.
Keiko Tanaka is the matriarch; she and her children Yuki and Haruto, together with her husband Hiroshi, are described as guardians of ancient rituals.
Keiko Tanaka says, "Our family tradition serves as the thread connecting us to our ancestors."
'Osoji' is a thorough year-end cleaning that purifies the living space to welcome the gods of the new year.
The family decorates the house with 'kadomatsu' (bamboo and pine decorations) and 'shimenawa' (sacred straw ropes), which symbolize the sanctity and prosperity of the home.
'Osechi ryori' is packed in multi-tiered boxes called 'jubako'; Kazunoko stands for fertility, Kuromame for health, and Datemaki for knowledge.
Hiroshi Tanaka prepares 'Toso,' a medicinal spiced sake believed to keep away evil spirits and illnesses for the year, using a recipe learned from his father.
The family visits Senso-ji in kimonos for 'Joya-no-Kane,' where the temple bell is rung 108 times to dispel the 108 temptations of this world.
Keiko says each bell ring reminds the family of their imperfections and that they must keep striving for self-improvement.
Senso-ji is reached through the 'Kaminarimon,' or 'Thunder Gate.'
After 'hatsumode' (the first shrine visit), the family plays 'Karuta,' racing to find cards with classical poetry known as 'hyakuninisshu.'
Haruto, the youngest, calls karuta "a memory and reflex exercise" that keeps alive the poetry of Japan's poets.
The family gathers around a heated 'kotatsu' to reflect on the year and discuss future goals.
Hiroshi says the traditions are a reminder of who they are and that the family has a duty to preserve their heritage.
